title: A review on the taxonomy, factors associated with sound absorption and theoretical modeling of porous sound absorbing materials
central_proposition: This paper provides a comprehensive review of sound absorbing materials, detailing their absorption mechanisms, classification, influencing factors, and theoretical modeling approaches to guide future research and material development.

concept_definitions.name: Sound
concept_definitions.definition: pressure variations (created by a vibrating object) that an ear can sense.

concept_definitions.name: Noise
concept_definitions.definition: a loud or unpleasant sound that causes a disturbance. It interferes the communication of another signal.

concept_definitions.name: Sound Absorption (SA)
concept_definitions.definition: mechanism of dissipation of sound energy within the material.

concept_definitions.name: Density (Bulk Density, pb)
concept_definitions.definition: the ratio between the in-vacuum mass of the porous aggregate and its bulk volume.

concept_definitions.name: Porosity (Φ)
concept_definitions.definition: the ratio of the open pores volume to the total volume.

concept_definitions.name: Tortuosity (α∞)
concept_definitions.definition: the measure of the elongation of the passageway through the pores, compared to the thickness of the sample.

concept_definitions.name: Air flow resistivity (σ)
concept_definitions.definition: the resistance experienced by air when it passes through a material.

concept_definitions.name: Thermal characteristic length (Λ')
concept_definitions.definition: describes the thermal dissipation effects at medium and high frequencies.

concept_definitions.name: Viscous characteristic length (Λ)
concept_definitions.definition: describes the effects of viscous dissipation at mid and high frequencies.

argument_structure: The paper systematically reviews sound absorbing materials by first explaining the fundamental sound absorption mechanism, then classifying existing materials based on fiber nature and macroscopic structure. It proceeds to detail key material properties (fiber size, thickness, density, porosity, tortuosity, air flow resistivity, air gap thickness, and characteristic lengths) that influence sound absorption. Finally, it discusses theoretical models for predicting acoustical behavior, provides a cost analysis, and outlines applications, concluding with insights for future material development.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Sound absorption occurs through the dissipation of sound energy within a material. This primarily happens as sound waves propagate through minute interconnected voids, leading to energy loss due to friction between air particles and the void walls. Additionally, internal reflections within the material contribute to energy transfer. The effectiveness of absorption is modulated by pore size, with larger pores generally increasing energy transfer and smaller pores increasing reflection. For optimal absorption, pressure waves must penetrate deeply into the material.

findings.antecedent: Sound waves propagating in porous material
findings.mechanism: Sound waves lose energy due to friction between air particles and the material's void walls, and through internal reflections within the material. Deeper penetration of pressure waves into the material facilitates greater interaction and energy transfer.
findings.quote: The sound wave loses its energy due to the friction between the air particles and the void walls. Also, there is an energy transfer because of internal reflections.
findings.empirical_support_cited: General understanding of sound absorption physics

findings.antecedent: Larger pore size in sound absorbing material
findings.mechanism: Larger pores facilitate increased energy transfer from the vibrating air particles to the solid structure of the material, leading to more effective sound absorption.
findings.quote: If the size of the pores is big, the energy transfer within the material is increased and hence more energy is absorbed by the material.

findings.antecedent: Smaller pore size in sound absorbing material
findings.mechanism: Smaller pores reduce the energy transfer from the vibrating air particles to the solid structure, causing more sound energy to be reflected from the surface rather than absorbed.
findings.quote: if the size of the pores is small, the transfer of energy into the solid structure decreases and hence more energy gets reflected from the surface, creating a lesser amount of useful acoustic absorption.

findings.antecedent: Reduction in fiber diameter of fibrous sound absorbing material
findings.mechanism: A reduction in fiber diameter necessitates more fibers for the same volume density, which in turn increases the air flow resistance and creates a more tortuous path for sound waves, leading to greater frictional energy dissipation.
findings.quote: The reduction in fiber diameter leads to rise in the value of the SAC (Fig. 11) because more fibers are required for the same volume density at the same thickness of the sample material. The result of a reduction in the fiber diameter is higher air flow resistance and more tortuous path.

findings.mechanism: Thicker materials are more effective at absorbing low-frequency sounds (longer wavelengths) because they provide a longer path for sound waves to interact with the material and dissipate energy. Optimal absorption occurs when thickness is at least one-tenth of the incident sound wavelength.
findings.quote: Thicker the material, higher the SAC (Fig. 12) and the effective SAC is accomplished when the material thickness is one-tenth of an incident sound wavelength.

findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) in the middle and high-frequency range
findings.mechanism: Increased material density leads to greater surface friction for sound waves, which enhances energy loss and thus improves sound absorption, particularly for higher frequencies (>2000 Hz).
findings.quote: The sound absorption value is increased in the middle and high-frequency range due to an increase in the density (Fig. 13). The SAC is increased because the energy loss increases due to the increase in surface friction.

findings.antecedent: Porosity (open pores volume) of porous material
findings.mechanism: Sufficient open porosity is essential for sound waves to penetrate the material's surface and interact with its internal structure, allowing for energy dissipation through friction. The number, size, and type of open pores are critical determinants.
findings.quote: The porosity is necessary for sound dissipation by friction and this is possible because of enough pores on the material surface for sound to pass through and get diminished.

findings.antecedent: Tortuosity of material (elongation of passageway through pores)
findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) at higher frequencies
findings.mechanism: Increased tortuosity forces sound waves to travel a longer, more circuitous path within the material, leading to greater interaction with pore walls and enhanced energy dissipation through friction, particularly effective at higher frequencies.
findings.quote: If the tortuosity has increased, the SAC increases monotonously towards higher frequency side (peak of SAC).

findings.mechanism: Air flow resistivity governs the ease with which air enters a porous structure and the resistance it encounters. An optimal resistivity allows for sufficient air movement and friction for energy dissipation; values that are too low (little resistance) or too high (blocked flow) result in reduced absorption.
findings.quote: The air flow resistivity is the resistance experienced by air when it passes through a material. It determines both the SA and sound transmitting properties of the material... A smaller value shows little resistance to air flowing through the material, whereas a higher value is a sign that the material pores are so close that air flow is blocked, and therefore, a low value of sound absorption may be anticipated.

findings.antecedent: Air gap thickness behind sound absorbing material
findings.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) in mid and higher frequencies
findings.mechanism: A greater air gap allows sound waves to be trapped longer, leading to more energy loss and enhanced sound absorption, particularly effective in the mid and higher frequency ranges.
findings.quote: There is a more energy loss with a greater density of fibers as compared to that with the smaller density because sound passing through the material might be trapped longer in the air gap. The SAC increases in mid and higher frequencies as air gap thickness increases.

findings.antecedent: Air gap layer brought closer to a rigid backing
findings.mechanism: Reducing the distance of the air gap layer to a rigid backing diminishes the effectiveness of the air gap in trapping and dissipating sound energy.
findings.quote: performance decreases when the air gap layer is brought closer to the rigid backing.

findings.antecedent: Thermal characteristic length (Λ') of porous material
findings.mechanism: The thermal characteristic length represents the average radius of larger cells where thermal losses are dominant over viscous losses, indicating the material's capacity for thermal energy dissipation at medium and high frequencies.
findings.quote: The thermal characteristic length in Fig. 19a describes the thermal dissipation effects at medium and high frequencies [138].

findings.antecedent: Viscous characteristic length (Λ) of porous material
findings.mechanism: The viscous characteristic length represents the average radius of smaller cells and necks where viscous losses are dominant over thermal losses, indicating the material's capacity for viscous energy dissipation at medium and high frequencies.
findings.quote: The viscous characteristic length in Fig. 19b describes the effects of viscous dissipation at mid and high frequencies [138].

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: New acoustic materials designed with reduced fiber diameter will exhibit increased Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC).
Increasing the thickness of a porous sound absorbing material will lead to a higher Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC), particularly for low-frequency sounds.

Optimizing the density of porous materials will enhance Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC), with denser materials performing better at higher frequencies and less dense materials at lower frequencies.
Materials with higher open porosity will demonstrate greater sound energy dissipation and thus higher Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC).
Increasing the tortuosity of a material's pore structure will lead to an increased Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) at higher frequencies.
An optimal air flow resistivity range exists for porous materials that maximizes Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC), with values too low or too high resulting in reduced absorption.
Increasing the air gap thickness behind a sound absorbing material will improve its Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) in mid and high-frequency ranges.

Materials with specific thermal and viscous characteristic lengths can be designed to optimize thermal and viscous dissipation effects, respectively, at medium and high frequencies, leading to improved sound absorption.
bridge_warrants: The physical mechanisms of sound absorption (e.g., energy dissipation, friction, internal reflections) directly contribute to reducing unwanted sensory input ('noise'), which aligns with the Predictive Processing framework's goal of minimizing prediction error and maintaining a stable internal state for human well-being.
methodological_critiques: Empirical models for sound absorption are considered simple approximations, often using power-law relations derived from best-fitting experimental data, which may limit their precision or generalizability.

Empirical models often simplify pore geometry to cylindrical shapes, which is a limitation given the complex and irregular nature of actual pore shapes in porous materials, making exact modeling difficult.
model_structure: The paper describes two main categories of theoretical models for porous materials: 1) Empirical models, which are simpler and primarily require air flow resistivity to estimate characteristic impedance and complex propagation constant (e.g., Delany-Bazley, Miki). 2) Phenomenological models, which are more complex and require additional parameters such as porosity, viscous characteristic length, thermal characteristic length, and tortuosity to predict acoustical behavior, assuming either a rigid or flexible material skeleton (e.g., Johnson-Champoux-Allard, Biot).
limitations: Synthetic sound absorbing materials, despite their excellent performance, pose environmental concerns due to their production processes involving high-temperature extrusion and petrochemical sources, leading to a noticeable carbon footprint.
The higher cost of synthetic fibers compared to natural fibers presents a practical limitation for their widespread adoption in sound absorbing products.
